articleTitle: Why Airlines Love Overbooking: The $4.2 Billion mathematical loophole behind selling 115% seat capac
summary: Why Airlines Love Overbooking: The $4.2 Billion mathematical loophole behind selling 115% seat capacity on peak routes and legal rights to 400% cash payouts.

systemMechanisms.name: Sell confirmed travel
systemMechanisms.operation: A customer purchases travel, but some booked customers later change flights or fail to appear. Flexible-ticket changes are one reason a nominally full booking list can produce empty seats.
systemMechanisms.economicMeaning: Booking demand and the number of passengers who actually board are different quantities.

systemMechanisms.name: Forecast missing passengers
systemMechanisms.operation: The airline predicts no-shows and sells additional reservations to offset them. DOT identifies this as the purpose of overselling.
systemMechanisms.economicMeaning: Extra reservations can fill seats that otherwise would depart empty.

systemMechanisms.name: Balance revenue against displacement costs
systemMechanisms.operation: The economic rationale is that compensating some displaced customers can cost less than repeatedly leaving seats empty. DOT identifies revenue enhancement and operational efficiency as benefits of the permitted practice.​
systemMechanisms.economicMeaning: Analytical synthesis: additional retained revenue must be evaluated against compensation, alternative transportation and other incremental costs. None of the retrieved evidence establishes a $4.2 billion net benefit.

systemMechanisms.name: Resolve actual attendance
systemMechanisms.operation: When more passengers are ready to fly than available seats, the airline must first solicit volunteers before involuntarily denying boarding.
systemMechanisms.economicMeaning: The uncertain booking decision becomes an immediate capacity problem.

systemMechanisms.name: Negotiate voluntary displacement
systemMechanisms.operation: Passengers can negotiate money or vouchers for surrendering their seats. There is no limit on the amount an airline may offer volunteers; voucher restrictions must be disclosed.
systemMechanisms.economicMeaning: The airline obtains a seat through a negotiated agreement rather than automatically applying the involuntary-compensation schedule.

systemMechanisms.name: Apply boarding priorities if volunteers are insufficient
systemMechanisms.operation: The airline may select passengers using fair boarding priorities, including check-in time, fare paid or frequent-flyer status. It must provide involuntarily bumped passengers a written explanation of their rights and its selection criteria.
systemMechanisms.economicMeaning: The remaining capacity shortfall is allocated to specific passengers.

systemMechanisms.name: Pay eligible compensation
systemMechanisms.operation: Calculate compensation using the applicable fare and the planned arrival time of offered substitute transportation. Offer payment at the airport that day; if substitute transportation leaves before payment can be made, pay within 24 hours of the incident.​
systemMechanisms.economicMeaning: Statutory compensation is a cost of eligible involuntary displacement, not a universal payment for every oversold booking.

systemMechanisms.name: Report the outcome accurately
systemMechanisms.operation: Reporting carriers submit quarterly denied-boarding information. Accepting a voucher after involuntary denial does not convert the passenger into a volunteer; DOT enforced this distinction against Spirit.
systemMechanisms.economicMeaning: Classification affects both the passenger-rights record and public comparisons of airline performance.

editorialVerdict.summary: Overbooking is a documented, explicitly regulated business practice—not a newly discovered legal loophole. Airlines sell beyond physical capacity to offset anticipated no-shows, then seek volunteers or compensate eligible passengers when too many arrive. The proposed $4.2 billion revenue figure and 115% peak-route booking claim were not substantiated by this research.​

editorialVerdict.jurisdiction: United States. The compensation rules described here concern covered departures from U.S. airports, not universal passenger rights or Swiss law.
